kurals.tamil:
சிறப்பீனும் செல்வம் பெறினும் பிறர்க்குஇன்னா
செய்யாமை மாசற்றார் கோள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Sirappeenum selvam perinum pirarkku innaa
Seyyaamai maasatraar kol.
kurals.meaning: Even if hurting someone would win them wealth great enough to bring honour and prestige, people whose minds are free of stain hold firmly to the rule of never causing pain to others.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone offers you a huge treasure chest, but only if you push another kid down to get it. A truly good person says “no thanks” every time. Valluvar says the pure-hearted never hurt anyone, not even for the biggest prize in the world.
kurals.university: The chapter opens by testing the principle of non-harm against its strongest temptation: sirappu eenum selvam, wealth that “gives birth to” distinction and social standing. The word kol (settled principle, fixed resolve) matters: non-harm is presented not as a mood or a calculation but as a standing commitment of the maasatraar, “those without stain,” whose minds are clear of the anger and greed that make harm seem attractive. Placed in the turavaraviyal (the section on the renunciant’s virtues), the couplet implies that the refusal to profit from another’s suffering is a defining mark of spiritual maturity, not merely of good manners. The same structure appears in Cicero’s Stoic claim that profiting by a neighbour’s loss is more contrary to nature than death or poverty, and in Plato’s thought-experiment of the Ring of Gyges, which asks whether anyone would stay just if injustice were profitable and safe. Valluvar’s answer is that the stainless would.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him avoid (the acquisition of) wealth and (the gratification of his) desires, if they are opposed to the sacred law, and even lawful acts which may cause pain in the future or are offensive to men.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the householder to give up wealth and pleasures whenever getting them would go against dharma, and even to avoid legal acts that would cause pain or offend others.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Manu ranks not-causing-pain above getting rich: wealth gained against righteousness or at others’ cost is to be refused.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong structural match (renounce wealth that conflicts with dharma or causes pain); Manu frames it as law for the householder rather than as the mark of the pure-hearted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that no amount of worldly gain is worth the loss of one’s inner life.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts set the greatest possible riches against moral integrity and find the riches not worth it. Valluvar names harming others as the price the pure refuse to pay.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘not even for the whole world’ logic; does not specifically mention harming others as the means of gain.

islam.quote_or_event: “O believers! Do not devour one another’s wealth illegally, but rather trade by mutual consent.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids enriching yourself at another person’s expense by unjust means; wealth must change hands only by fair, willing exchange.
islam.tie_back: Both forbid seeking wealth through another’s loss or pain. The Kural adds that the pure refuse such gain even when it would bring prestige.
islam.source: Qur’an 4:29 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on refusing wealth gained by harming others; framed as a legal prohibition rather than a character ideal.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is a little with righteousness than great revenues without right.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that a small, honest income is worth more than a fortune gained unjustly.
judaism.tie_back: Same weighing as the Kural: great revenue on one side, righteousness on the other, and righteousness wins.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on preferring righteousness over great wealth; ‘without right’ is broader than ‘by harming others.’

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He is indeed virtuous, wise, and righteous who neither for his own sake nor for the sake of another (does any wrong), who does not crave for sons, wealth, or kingdom, and does not desire success by unjust means.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the truly wise person as one who will do no wrong for any reason, and who does not seek wealth or success by unjust means.
buddhism.tie_back: Nearly the Kural’s own claim: the pure person will not do wrong even when wealth or success is the reward.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close: explicitly refuses wrongdoing even for wealth or kingdom.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Plato’s retelling of the myth, the shepherd Gyges finds a gold ring that makes him invisible. Freed from all consequences, he seduces the queen, kills the king, and takes the throne. Glaucon uses the tale to ask whether anyone would stay just if injustice were profitable and could never be discovered.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Ring of Gyges tests whether people avoid harming others only because they fear getting caught.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural gives the answer Socrates goes on to defend: the truly pure refuse to harm others for gain even when the gain is huge and the harm would go unpunished.
greek_mythology.source: Plato, Republic II, 359c–360d (the Ring of Gyges)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The myth poses the Kural’s exact test (harm for great gain); Gyges himself fails it, so the parallel works by contrast.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Well then, for a man to take something from his neighbour and to profit by his neighbour's loss is more contrary to Nature than is death or poverty or pain or anything else that can affect either our person or our property.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero argues that gaining at another’s expense is worse, and more against human nature, than suffering any personal loss.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero and Valluvar both say the good person would rather stay poor than get rich by hurting someone else.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis III.21 (trans. Walter Miller, Loeb 1913)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close: explicitly ranks not profiting from another’s loss above one’s own wealth.

kurals.tamil:
கறுத்துஇன்னா செய்தவக் கண்ணும் மறுத்தின்னா
செய்யாமை மாசற்றார் கோள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Karuththu innaa seydhavak kannum maruththu innaa
Seyyaamai maasatraar kol.
kurals.meaning: Even when someone, out of spite, has done them harm, the stainless make it their rule not to hurt that person in return.
kurals.elementary: If a kid on the playground knocks over your sandcastle on purpose, it is tempting to knock over theirs too. This kural says good-hearted people don’t pay back hurt with more hurt, even when the other person started it.
kurals.university: Where Kural 311 tested non-harm against greed, 312 tests it against the stronger pull of justified grievance. Karuththu describes the other party’s grudging, hostile intent, while maruththu (in return, in retort) names the retaliatory impulse the stainless decline. The couplet repeats the closing phrase of 311 word for word (seyyaamai maasatraar kol), binding the two into a pair: neither profit nor provocation licenses harm. This places Valluvar alongside Socrates in the Crito, who startled his friend by insisting that one must not return injury for injury, and alongside the Sermon on the Mount and the Buddha’s Simile of the Saw. It also stands in contrast to the older Greek ethic of helping friends and harming enemies, which Plato’s Socrates set out to dismantle.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not envious but is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor and is free from false ego, who is equal in both happiness and distress, who is tolerant … such a devotee of Mine is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna praises the person who bears no hatred toward any being, stays friendly and compassionate, and is patient and forgiving.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s stainless person and the Gita’s dear devotee share the same trait: no hostility toward anyone, even those who give cause.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Describes the non-hating, forgiving disposition but does not explicitly address retaliation against someone who has done harm.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Recompense to no man evil for evil. Provide things honest in the sight of all men.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers never to pay back evil with evil.
christianity.tie_back: Almost the Kural in one line: do not return harm, even to one who harmed you first.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match: explicit prohibition of retaliating harm for harm.

islam.quote_or_event: “If you raise your hand to kill me, I will not raise mine to kill you, because I fear Allah—the Lord of all worlds.”
islam.explanation: One of Adam’s two sons, threatened by his jealous brother, says he will not strike back even to defend himself.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s stainless person, Adam’s son refuses to answer hostility with hostility, even under the gravest threat.
islam.source: Qur’an 5:28 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel of refusing to retaliate against a hostile aggressor.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids taking revenge or even holding a grudge, and commands love of neighbour instead.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts forbid repaying the one who wronged you. Leviticus adds that the grudge itself must go.
judaism._accuracy_note: Direct prohibition of revenge; framed for ‘the children of thy people’ rather than universally.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, even if bandits were to carve you up savagely into pieces with a two-handled saw, he among you who let his heart get angered even at that would not be doing my bidding.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Simile of the Saw, the Buddha tells his monks that even under the most brutal attack they must not give way to anger or ill will toward the attackers.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural forbids returning harm to a malicious attacker. The Buddha goes further and forbids even the inner anger that would motivate it.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 21, Kakacupama Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Extreme and vivid form of the same non-retaliation principle; stresses inner non-anger more than outward non-harm.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles’ Ajax, Odysseus has been Ajax’s bitterest enemy, and Ajax tried to kill him. After Ajax’s suicide, Agamemnon and Menelaus want to leave the body unburied as revenge. Odysseus, the injured party, overrules them and insists his enemy be buried with honour.
greek_mythology.explanation: The man with the most reason to seek revenge is the one who refuses it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus acts as the Kural’s stainless person: wronged by a hostile man, he will not harm him in return, even in death.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear instance of declining revenge on an enemy; the harm refused is posthumous dishonour, not direct injury.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to anyone, whatever evil we may have suffered from him.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates, in prison awaiting execution, insists that wronging someone is never right, even as payback for a wrong done to us.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates and Valluvar state the same rule in almost the same words: no harm in return, whatever harm was suffered.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match: explicit prohibition on returning evil for evil.

kurals.tamil:
செய்யாமல் செற்றார்க்கும் இன்னாத செய்தபின்
உய்யா விழுமந் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Seyyaamal setraarkkum innaadha seydhapin
Uyyaa vizhumam tharum.
kurals.meaning: Even toward people who hated and harmed you when you had done nothing to them, if you strike back with harm, it will afterwards bring you sorrow you cannot escape.
kurals.elementary: Suppose someone is mean to you for no reason at all, and you get them back. It might feel fair for a minute, but later you end up feeling awful and stuck in a big fight. The kural says hitting back, even when you didn’t start it, brings trouble you can’t get out of.
kurals.university: This couplet sharpens 312 by removing every excuse: the victim did nothing (seyyaamal) to provoke the enmity (setraar, those who hate). Even so, retaliating yields uyyaa vizhumam, a grief from which there is no escape. Because the chapter belongs to the section on the renunciant, older commentators and Pope’s translation read it as addressed to the ascetic, for whom retaliation undoes the discipline of years; the ‘inescapable sorrow’ is at once moral self-damage and the karmic consequence of the act. The logic is prudential as well as ethical: revenge draws the avenger into the cycle of harm. Greek tragedy dramatises exactly this spiral in the house of Atreus, and the Gospel compresses it into the saying that those who take the sword perish by it.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If (the punishment falls) not on (the offender) himself, (it falls) on his sons, if not on the sons, (at least) on his grandsons; but an iniquity (once) committed, never fails to produce fruit to him who wrought it.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu teaches that a wrong, once done, always bears fruit for the one who did it, even if the result is delayed.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘inescapable sorrow’ is this law applied to retaliation: harm done in revenge is still harm, and its fruit cannot be avoided.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the inescapability of consequences; speaks of wrongdoing generally, not specifically of retaliation against an aggressor.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.”
christianity.explanation: When Peter strikes one of the men arresting Jesus, Jesus orders him to stop, warning that violence returns on those who use it.
christianity.tie_back: Peter is retaliating against men who came against an innocent Jesus, the Kural’s exact situation, and Jesus warns that such retaliation brings ruin on the one who strikes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match: retaliation against unprovoked aggressors, with a warning that the harm rebounds.

islam.quote_or_event: “The reward of an evil deed is its equivalent. But whoever pardons and seeks reconciliation, then their reward is with Allah.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an allows proportionate response to a wrong, but holds up pardon and reconciliation as the better and more rewarded path.
islam.tie_back: Both texts steer the wronged person away from retaliation. The Kural warns of the sorrow revenge brings; the Qur’an promises reward for forgiving instead.
islam.source: Qur’an 42:40 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Partial: the Qur’an permits equivalent retribution while preferring pardon; the Kural treats retaliation as self-harming without exception.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Say not thou, I will recompense evil; but wait on the LORD, and he shall save thee.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs tells the wronged person not to plan revenge but to leave the matter to God.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts tell the victim of unprovoked harm not to repay it; Proverbs adds that deliverance lies in restraint, not in revenge.
judaism._accuracy_note: Clear prohibition of revenge; the Kural’s emphasis on the avenger’s own ruin is implicit rather than stated.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that answering hatred with hatred only keeps it alive; only non-hatred ends it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural says retaliation traps the avenger in lasting sorrow; the Dhammapada explains why: hatred returned only feeds the cycle.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Captures the self-perpetuating nature of retaliation; less explicit about the avenger’s personal suffering.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the myth behind Aeschylus’ Agamemnon, Thyestes wrongs his brother Atreus, and Atreus takes revenge by serving Thyestes his own children at a feast. The revenge does not end the feud; it plants a curse that brings murder upon murder through the next generations of the house.
greek_mythology.explanation: Atreus answers a real wrong with revenge, and the revenge brings disaster on his own family for generations.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ‘inescapable sorrow’ made into a family history: harm returned for harm becomes a curse on the avenger’s own line.
greek_mythology.source: Aeschylus, Agamemnon 1583–1602 (Aegisthus’ account of the feast of Thyestes)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of retaliation rebounding on the avenger; Atreus had been wronged, though not wholly unprovoked in every version.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong doer.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius advises that the real victory over someone who wrongs you is refusing to become like them.
philosophy.tie_back: Both see revenge as a trap: the Kural warns that it brings inescapable sorrow, and Marcus says it turns you into the very wrongdoer you resent.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the view that retaliation damages the avenger; the damage is to character rather than to later fortune.

kurals.tamil:
இன்னாசெய் தாரை ஒறுத்தல் அவர்நாண
நன்னயஞ் செய்து விடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Innaa seydhaarai oruththal avar naana
Nannayam seydhu vidal.
kurals.meaning: The true way to punish those who have harmed you is to do them such kindness that they feel ashamed, and then to let the matter go.
kurals.elementary: If your brother breaks your toy and you share your snack with him anyway, he will probably feel really sorry about the toy. Valluvar says that is the best “punishment”: being so kind that the person feels ashamed of being mean, and then forgetting about it.
kurals.university: Perhaps the most quoted couplet of the chapter, 314 redefines punishment itself. Oruththal (to punish, chastise) is kept as the goal, but the means is nannayam (goodness, benefit), and its effect is naanam, the wrongdoer’s shame. The closing word vidal (to leave off, let go) led Parimelazhagar and later commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan to read the couplet as requiring one to forget both the injury received and the good returned, so that the kindness does not become a hidden weapon. The idea is found across traditions: Proverbs and Paul speak of heaping coals of fire on an enemy’s head by feeding him, and the Qur’an promises that repelling evil with what is better can turn an enemy into a close friend. What Valluvar adds is the paradox that the gentlest act is the most effective sanction.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When One injures another, the injured turns round and injures the injurer. Similarly, when one cherishes another, that other cherishes the cherisher. One should frame one's rule of conduct according to this.”
hinduism.explanation: Brihaspati tells Yudhishthira that harm invites harm in return while kindness invites kindness, and that one should build one’s conduct on this.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s strategy of answering harm with kindness uses this same principle: goodness shown draws goodness out of the other person.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Section 113 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Gives the reciprocity principle behind the Kural’s strategy but does not describe returning kindness to someone who has already harmed you.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head. Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to meet an enemy’s need with kindness, which will bring the enemy to burning shame, and so to overcome evil with good.
christianity.tie_back: This is almost the Kural itself: the ‘coals of fire’ are the shame the kindness produces, and the punishment is goodness.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match: kindness to an enemy producing shame, and evil overcome by good.

islam.quote_or_event: “Good and evil cannot be equal. Respond ˹to evil˺ with what is best, then the one you are in a feud with will be like a close friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells believers to answer wrongdoing with the finest possible conduct, which can turn a bitter enemy into a devoted friend.
islam.tie_back: Both texts answer harm with goodness and expect it to change the wrongdoer. The Kural stresses the enemy’s shame, the Qur’an the enemy’s transformation into a friend.
islam.source: Qur’an 41:34 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Very close in method and expected outcome.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink: For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the LORD shall reward thee.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs advises feeding a hungry enemy, which will heap burning shame on him, and promises that God will reward the kindness.
judaism.tie_back: The source of Paul’s later saying, and a close match to the Kural: kindness to one who harmed you produces shame in him.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close; lacks the Kural’s instruction to then forget the whole affair.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Overcome the angry by non-anger; overcome the wicked by goodness; overcome the miser by generosity; overcome the liar by truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that each vice is best conquered by its opposite virtue, so wickedness is conquered by goodness.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts treat goodness as the true way to defeat someone who does wrong.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on overcoming the wicked through goodness; does not mention shame.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the close of Aeschylus’ Eumenides, the Furies threaten to poison Athens after Orestes is acquitted. Athena does not fight or punish them. She answers their rage with patient persuasion and offers of honour and a home in the city, until they give up their anger and become the Kindly Ones.
greek_mythology.explanation: Athena defeats the hostile Furies not by force but by generosity and respect.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ideal, Athena answers hostility with kindness, and the kindness, not punishment, ends the conflict.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good illustration of kindness overcoming hostility; the Furies are won over rather than shamed.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “One thing here is worth a great deal, to pass thy life in truth and justice, with a benevolent disposition even to liars and unjust men.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius says the one thing of real worth is to live truly and justly while keeping goodwill even toward liars and the unjust.
philosophy.tie_back: Both call for positive goodwill toward those who do wrong, not just the absence of revenge.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the benevolence toward wrongdoers; does not present kindness as a form of punishment that produces shame.

kurals.tamil:
அறிவினான் ஆகுவ துண்டோ பிறிதின்நோய்
தந்நோய்போல் போற்றாக் கடை.
kurals.transliteration:
Arivinaan aaguvadhu undo piridhin noy
Thannoy pol potraak kadai.
kurals.meaning: What good is all one’s knowledge if one does not treat another creature’s pain as one’s own and guard it against suffering?
kurals.elementary: You might know lots of facts, like all the planets or every dinosaur. But if your friend falls and scrapes their knee and you don’t care, what good are all those facts? Valluvar says being smart only matters if you feel other people’s hurt like it’s your own.
kurals.university: Valluvar here makes empathy the test of knowledge. Arivu (knowledge, understanding) is asked to justify itself, and the only acceptable answer is that it leads one to regard piridhin noy, the pain of another (piridhu can mean any other being, not only humans), as thannoy, one’s own pain. The verb potru (to guard, protect, cherish) makes the demand active: it is not enough to feel sympathy, one must protect the other from harm as one protects oneself. This anticipates a recurring theme in the Kural that learning without moral application is barren. Comparable ideas appear in the Bhagavad Gita’s claim that true knowledge produces equal vision of all beings, in the Buddha’s reflection that since everyone holds themselves dear no one should harm another, and in the Stoic doctrine of oikeiosis, which asks us to draw the circle of concern outward until strangers are treated as kin.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The humble sages, by virtue of true knowledge, see with equal vision a learned and gentle brāhmaṇa, a cow, an elephant, a dog and a dog-eater [outcaste].”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says real knowledge shows itself in seeing all beings, high or low, human or animal, with the same eye.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts judge knowledge by its moral fruit: the truly wise see every being as equal, and so cannot treat another’s pain as less real than their own.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Links true knowledge to equal regard for all beings; does not explicitly speak of feeling others’ pain.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him,”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus’ parable, a priest and a Levite, both religious experts, walk past a wounded man, but a despised Samaritan feels his pain and cares for him.
christianity.tie_back: The parable makes the Kural’s point in story form: religious learning is useless if it does not lead you to treat another’s pain as your own.
christianity.source: Luke 10:33 (KJV), Parable of the Good Samaritan
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong parallel: the learned pass by while compassion is shown by another; the verse quoted is one line of a longer parable.

islam.quote_or_event: “The similitude of believers in regard to mutual love, affection, fellow-feeling is that of one body; when any limb of it aches, the whole body aches, because of sleeplessness and fever.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares the community of believers to a single body in which one part’s pain is felt by all.
islam.tie_back: Both call for feeling another’s pain as your own; the hadith makes it literal through the image of one body.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close on shared suffering; framed for the community of believers rather than for all creatures, and does not mention knowledge.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Eliezer said: Let the honor of your friend be as dear to you as your own”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Eliezer teaches that another person’s dignity should matter to you as much as your own.
judaism.tie_back: Both require treating what belongs to another, whether honour or well-being, as if it were your own.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:10 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Same self-other equivalence, but applied to honour rather than to pain.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Searching all directions with your awareness, you find no one dearer than yourself. In the same way, others are thickly dear to themselves. So you shouldn't hurt others if you love yourself.”
buddhism.explanation: After King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika agree that no one is dearer to them than themselves, the Buddha draws the conclusion: others feel the same, so do not harm them.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural and the Buddha reason the same way: understanding how precious you are to yourself should make you protect others as you protect yourself.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close: insight into one’s own self-love grounds the duty not to harm others.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the opening of Sophocles’ Ajax, Athena shows Odysseus his enemy Ajax, driven mad and humiliated. She invites him to gloat, but Odysseus says he pities Ajax though he is a foe, because in Ajax’s ruin he sees his own fate and that of all mortals.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus recognises his enemy’s suffering as the kind of suffering that could be his own.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s insight in action: true understanding shows up as feeling another’s pain as one’s own, even an enemy’s.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear case of empathy grounded in shared mortality; Odysseus pities rather than actively protects.

philosophy.quote_or_event: The Stoic Hierocles pictures each person at the centre of concentric circles (self, family, fellow citizens, all humanity) and urges us to keep drawing the outer circles inward, treating those far away as if they were near.
philosophy.explanation: Stoic oikeiosis teaches that moral progress means extending to others the care we naturally feel for ourselves.
philosophy.tie_back: Hierocles offers a method for the Kural’s demand: widen self-concern until another’s pain is guarded as one’s own.
philosophy.source: Hierocles the Stoic, fragment in Stobaeus, Anthology 4.27.23
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in spirit (extending self-care to others); it describes a gradual discipline rather than a test of knowledge.

kurals.tamil:
இன்னா எனத்தான் உணர்ந்தவை துன்னாமை
வேண்டும் பிறன்கண் செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Innaa enaththaan unarndhavai thunnaamai
Vendum piran kan seyal.
kurals.meaning: Whatever you have learned from your own experience to be painful, you must never do to another person.
kurals.elementary: Remember how much it hurt when someone left you out of a game? Then you already know not to leave anyone else out. This kural says: if something hurt you, don’t do it to others.
kurals.university: This is Valluvar’s clearest statement of the negative Golden Rule, and it is regularly cited alongside Hillel and the Mahabharata in comparative discussions of that principle. The phrase thaan unarndhavai, ‘what one has oneself felt or known,’ grounds the rule in lived experience rather than abstract principle: each person’s own suffering is a textbook of what not to do. Thunnaamai (not approaching, not engaging in) makes the prohibition wide enough to cover even drawing near to such acts. Unlike the positive form (‘do unto others’), the negative form sets a minimum that anyone can meet, and so needs no guesswork about what others want. It closely matches Brihaspati’s summary of dharma in the Mahabharata, Hillel’s one-sentence Torah, and Isocrates’ advice to the Cyprians.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One should never do that to another which one regards as injurious to one's own self. This, in brief, is the rule of Righteousness.”
hinduism.explanation: Brihaspati sums up all of dharma for Yudhishthira in one rule: never do to others what you would find harmful to yourself.
hinduism.tie_back: An almost word-for-word counterpart of the Kural: what you know hurts you, do not do to others.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Section 113 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match of the negative Golden Rule.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus sums up the Law and the Prophets as treating others the way you want to be treated.
christianity.tie_back: The positive form of the Kural’s rule; both use one’s own experience as the measure of how to treat others.
christianity._accuracy_note: Same principle in positive form; the Kural states the negative (prohibitive) version.

islam.quote_or_event: “None of you will have faith till he wishes for his (Muslim) brother what he likes for himself.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes wishing for others what you wish for yourself a condition of true faith.
islam.tie_back: Both use one’s own desires and aversions as the standard for how to treat others.
islam._accuracy_note: Golden Rule in positive form; framed for one’s brother in faith.

judaism.quote_or_event: “That which is hateful to you do not do to another; that is the entire Torah, and the rest is its interpretation. Go study.”
judaism.explanation: Asked to teach the whole Torah while standing on one foot, Hillel gives the negative Golden Rule.
judaism.tie_back: Hillel and Valluvar give the same rule in the same negative form: do not do to others what you yourself find painful.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a (William Davidson Edition, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match of the negative Golden Rule.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hurt not others in ways that you yourself would find hurtful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Udanavarga states the negative Golden Rule directly.
buddhism.tie_back: Nearly identical to the Kural: let your own experience of hurt tell you what never to do to others.
buddhism.source: Udanavarga 5.18 (as quoted in comparative Golden Rule literature)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Content is a near-exact match. The English wording was verified only through a secondary source (Wikipedia’s Golden Rule article), not against a primary translation, so it is flagged for further checking.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Homer’s Odyssey, when the nymph Calypso finally agrees to let Odysseus leave, he suspects a trap. She swears she is planning for him only what she would plan for herself in the same need, since her mind is just and her heart is not made of iron.
greek_mythology.explanation: Calypso uses her own needs as the measure of how she treats Odysseus.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An early Greek example of the Golden Rule: treat another as you would want to be treated in their place, the principle behind the Kural.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Expresses the positive, self-as-measure form in a narrative setting; not a general prohibition of harm.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Do not do to others that which angers you when they do it to you.”
philosophy.explanation: Isocrates, writing as King Nicocles, advises his subjects to use their own resentment as a guide to how they should treat others.
philosophy.tie_back: A classical Greek statement of the same negative rule as the Kural.
philosophy.source: Isocrates, Nicocles (or The Cyprians) 61 (trans. George Norlin)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match of the negative Golden Rule.

kurals.tamil:
எனைத்தானும் எஞ்ஞான்றும் யார்க்கும் மனத்தானாம்
மாணாசெய் யாமை தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Enaiththaanum ennaandrum yaarkkum manaththaanaam
Maanaa seyyaamai thalai.
kurals.meaning: Never to do any unworthy harm, however small, at any time, to anyone, not even in one’s thoughts, is the highest virtue.
kurals.elementary: Some people only stop themselves from hitting. This kural asks for much more: don’t hurt anyone, not a little bit, not ever, and don’t even plan mean things in your head. That, it says, is the very best kind of goodness.
kurals.university: The couplet universalises the prohibition along every axis at once: degree (enaiththaanum, in any measure however small), time (ennaandrum, at any time), and person (yaarkkum, to anyone). The fourth axis is inward: manaththaan aam, ‘that which arises from the mind,’ which commentators read either as deliberate, knowing harm or as harm committed even in intention. Maanaa means base or ignoble acts. Calling this thalai (the head, the foremost virtue) places total non-harm at the top of the chapter’s ethical hierarchy. Similar demands to extend the prohibition into the inner life appear in Leviticus’ command not to hate one’s brother in the heart, in the First Letter of John, where hatred is equated with murder, and in the Metta Sutta’s wish that no one should even desire harm for another.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him not, even though in pain, (speak words) cutting (others) to the quick; let him not injure others in thought or deed; let him not utter speeches which make (others) afraid of him, since that will prevent him from gaining heaven.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu forbids injuring others by word, thought, or deed, even when one is suffering oneself.
hinduism.tie_back: Both extend the ban on harm to the mind itself: no injury in thought, word, or act.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on harm ‘in thought or deed’; lacks the Kural’s explicit ‘at any time, to anyone, however small.’

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him.”
christianity.explanation: The letter of John teaches that hatred in the heart is already murder in God’s eyes.
christianity.tie_back: Both move the line of harm from the hand to the mind: hostile intent is itself a wrong.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the inward extension of harm; less explicit about universality in time, degree, and person.

islam.quote_or_event: “There should be neither harming (darar) nor reciprocating harm (dirar).”
islam.explanation: This hadith lays down a general rule of Islamic ethics and law: no one may harm another, and harm may not be answered with harm.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it states a rule of non-harm without exceptions of person or occasion.
islam.source: An-Nawawi’s Forty Hadith, no. 32 (Ibn Majah; sunnah.com)
islam._accuracy_note: Universal prohibition of harm; does not extend explicitly to harm in thought.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids hatred even when it stays hidden in the heart.
judaism.tie_back: Both forbid harm at the level of the mind, not just outward acts.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on inner hostility; does not state the Kural’s universality across time and degree.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let none deceive another, or despise any being in any state. Let none through anger or ill-will wish harm upon another.”
buddhism.explanation: The Metta Sutta asks that no one deceive, despise, or even wish harm on any being.
buddhism.tie_back: Both reach from deed into wish: harming anyone, even in the mind, is ruled out.
buddhism.source: Karaniya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.8 (trans. Amaravati Sangha)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close: universal (‘any being in any state’) and extends to wishes.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus tells of Glaucus of Sparta, famed for honesty, who was holding money in trust and asked the Delphic oracle whether he might keep it by swearing a false oath. The Pythia answered that tempting the god with the question was as bad as doing the deed. Though he returned the money, his whole family line was later wiped out.
greek_mythology.explanation: The legend teaches that merely intending a wrong is already a serious wrong in the eyes of the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural forbids harm ‘even in the mind’; the Glaucus story shows the Greek conviction that intending harm already carries guilt.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on the guilt of intention; the harm contemplated is fraud rather than general injury.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Book I of the Republic, Socrates leads Polemarchus to abandon the traditional view that justice means helping friends and harming enemies. He argues that harming anyone makes them worse, and that it cannot be the work of the just man to harm anyone at all, friend or enemy.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates concludes that the just person harms no one, under any circumstances.
philosophy.tie_back: Both reject every exception to non-harm, including the traditional exception for enemies.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the universality (‘anyone at all’); does not treat harm in thought.

kurals.tamil:
தன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னாமை தானறிவான் என்கொலோ
மன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னா செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thannuyirkku innaamai thaan arivaan en kolo
Mannuyirkku innaa seyal.
kurals.meaning: A person knows well what pain feels like to his own life. Why, then, does he inflict that same pain on other living beings?
kurals.elementary: You know how much a bee sting hurts, because it happened to you. So why would anyone go around stinging others? This kural asks: if you know how pain feels, how can you give it to someone else?
kurals.university: Kural 318 turns the rule of 316 into a question, and the rhetorical form (en kolo, ‘why, then?’) exposes a contradiction in the person who harms. The contrast between thannuyir (one’s own life or self) and mannuyir (the lives that dwell on earth, all living beings) widens the circle beyond humans, in keeping with the Kural’s broad concern for all creatures, developed further in the next chapter on not killing. The argument is essentially one of consistency: whoever knows pain from the inside cannot claim not to know what they are doing when they cause it. Similar appeals to self-knowledge appear in the Gita’s ‘comparison to one’s own self,’ the Dhammapada’s instruction to put oneself in another’s place, and the Torah’s reminder that Israel knows the heart of the stranger because it was once a stranger.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He is a perfect yogī who, by comparison to his own self, sees the true equality of all beings, in both their happiness and their distress, O Arjuna!”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says the highest yogi uses his own experience of joy and sorrow to understand everyone else’s.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts ground concern for others in self-knowledge: your own distress tells you what others feel.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close on self-comparison as the basis of empathy; does not phrase it as a reproach to one who causes harm.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his followers to treat others exactly as they would want to be treated.
christianity.tie_back: Both make one’s own experience the measure of right treatment of others.
christianity._accuracy_note: Same self-as-measure principle; lacks the Kural’s rhetorical challenge to the one who already knows pain.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever wishes to be delivered from the fire and enter the garden should die with faith in Allah and the Last Day and should treat the people as he wishes to be treated by them.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes treating people as you wish to be treated a condition for salvation.
islam.tie_back: Both appeal to what one knows one wants, or does not want, for oneself as the guide for treating others.
islam._accuracy_note: Clear Golden Rule; positive form and embedded in a longer political hadith.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Also thou shalt not oppress a stranger: for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids oppressing strangers because Israel knows from its own history exactly how a stranger feels.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s argument: you know this pain yourself, so how can you inflict it on another?
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close: own experience of suffering is the explicit reason not to inflict it; applied to one category of person.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All tremble at violence; life is dear to all. Putting oneself in the place of another, one should not kill nor cause another to kill.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha reminds us that every being fears violence and loves life, so we should put ourselves in their place and never harm them.
buddhism.tie_back: Both reason from one’s own fear of harm to the duty not to harm any living being.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close; applies the principle especially to killing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the last book of the Iliad, old King Priam comes to Achilles to beg for the body of his son Hector. He asks Achilles to think of his own aged father. Achilles, remembering his father and his own grief, weeps with Priam and gives back the body.
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles stops abusing Hector’s body once he recognises Priam’s grief as the same grief his own father will feel.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles moves from inflicting pain to showing mercy exactly when he realises he knows that pain from the inside, the Kural’s point.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong dramatic parallel of self-knowledge of suffering ending the infliction of suffering.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “When asked how men might live most virtuously and most justly, he said, ‘If we never do ourselves what we blame in others.’”
philosophy.explanation: Thales, one of the Seven Sages, sums up the just life as never doing what we condemn when others do it.
philosophy.tie_back: Both expose the inconsistency of the one who harms: we know what we object to, so we must not do it ourselves.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 1.36 (Thales) (trans. C. D. Yonge)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Captures the consistency argument; speaks of blame rather than of experienced pain.

kurals.tamil:
பிறர்க்கின்னா முற்பகல் செய்யின் தமக்குஇன்னா
பிற்பகல் தாமே வரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pirarkku innaa murpagal seyyin thamakku innaa
Pirpagal thaame varum.
kurals.meaning: If you harm others in the morning, harm will come to you on its own by the afternoon.
kurals.elementary: It’s like throwing a ball hard against a wall: it bounces right back at you. This kural says being mean to someone in the morning means trouble will come bouncing back to you by the afternoon.
kurals.university: This is among the best-known couplets in Tamil, often quoted as a proverb. Its power lies in its compression of time: murpagal (forenoon) and pirpagal (afternoon) shrink the karmic interval, usually imagined across lifetimes, to a single day. The word thaame (of their own accord) makes the return automatic; no avenger or judge is named, and the consequence seems built into the act. The couplet thus combines a moral law with a psychological one, since harm tends to provoke retaliation and hostility quickly. Parallels range from the Mahabharata’s observation that the injured turns round and injures the injurer, to Proverbs’ image of the stone that rolls back on the one who pushes it, to Theseus giving each bandit on the road to Athens the death he dealt to others.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When One injures another, the injured turns round and injures the injurer.”
hinduism.explanation: Brihaspati warns Yudhishthira that harm done to another comes back to the one who did it.
hinduism.tie_back: The same law of return as the Kural: the harm you send out comes back to you.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Section 113 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close on the return of harm; lacks the Kural’s image of how quickly it comes.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that everyone harvests exactly what they have planted.
christianity.tie_back: Both teach that harm returns to its author; the Kural adds that the harvest comes fast.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on moral consequence; no specific emphasis on speed.

islam.quote_or_event: “If you act rightly, it is for your own good, but if you do wrong, it is to your own loss.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that the effects of one’s good and evil deeds fall back on oneself.
islam.tie_back: Both say that wrongdoing ultimately harms the wrongdoer.
islam.source: Qur’an 17:7 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Same principle of self-rebounding wrongdoing; no timing element, and set in a historical address to the Children of Israel.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs pictures harm as a pit that swallows the one who dug it, or a stone that rolls back on the one who pushed it.
judaism.tie_back: Both use the image of harm rebounding naturally on its maker, without any outside avenger.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close on the automatic return of harm; no mention of time.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like fine dust thrown against the wind, evil falls back upon that fool who offends an inoffensive, pure and guiltless man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares harming an innocent person to throwing dust into the wind: it blows straight back into your own face.
buddhism.tie_back: Both picture harm flying straight back at the one who sends it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Vivid match on immediate rebound; specified for harming the innocent.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On his journey to Athens, the young Theseus meets a series of bandits who torment travellers. He kills each one by the same method they used on their victims, bending Sinis’ pine trees, hurling Sciron off his cliff, and fitting Procrustes to his own bed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Each bandit suffers exactly the harm he used to inflict on others.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s law played out as myth: the harm each villain inflicted comes back to him in the same form.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good illustration of harm returning in kind; the return comes through a hero rather than ‘of its own accord.’

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Book IV of the Consolation of Philosophy, Lady Philosophy argues that goodness is what makes us human, so whoever abandons it stops being fully human and sinks into the likeness of a beast. Wickedness therefore is its own punishment and falls on the wicked at once.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius argues that evildoers are punished by their very wickedness, immediately and unavoidably.
philosophy.tie_back: Both see the harm done to others turning back on the doer without delay; Boethius places the punishment inside the soul.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book IV, prose 3
philosophy._accuracy_note: Captures immediacy and self-punishment; the penalty is inner degradation rather than outward misfortune.

kurals.tamil:
நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம் நோய்செய்யார்
நோயின்மை வேண்டு பவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Noyellaam noy seydhaar melavaam noy seyyaar
Noyinmai vendu pavar.
kurals.meaning: All suffering falls upon those who cause suffering; so those who wish to be free of suffering do not cause it to others.
kurals.elementary: If you plant thorns, you will get pricked walking through your own garden. If you never want to get pricked, don’t plant thorns. This kural says: if you want a life without pain, don’t give pain to anyone.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with a verbal tour de force: the word noy (pain, affliction, disease) appears four times in seven words, so that the sound of the couplet enacts its argument that pain circles back to its source. The first line states a law (all affliction settles on those who afflict), and the second draws the practical conclusion for anyone who wants noyinmai, freedom from suffering. The ethics of non-harm is here grounded partly in enlightened self-interest, rounding off a chapter that has moved from the stainless person’s principle (311–312), through empathy (315–318), to consequence (319–320). The idea is widely shared: Hesiod’s warning that the evil plotter harms himself most, the Qur’an’s statement that evil plotting backfires on the plotters, Marcus Aurelius’ remark that the wrongdoer wrongs himself, and the Dhammapada’s assurance that for one who does no evil there is no ill.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He by whom no one is put into difficulty and who is not disturbed by anyone, who is equipoised in happiness and distress, fear and anxiety, is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the ideal devotee as one who troubles no one and is troubled by no one.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita pairs the two halves of the Kural: the one who causes no distress is also the one free of distress.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Links not disturbing others with being undisturbed; does not state a law that suffering returns to its causer.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that the standard we apply to others will be applied to us.
christianity.tie_back: Both teach that what we deal out comes back to us, so the way to avoid harm is not to deal it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Clear reciprocity principle; framed around judging rather than inflicting pain.

islam.quote_or_event: “But evil plotting only backfires on those who plot.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an declares that evil schemes end up harming only the schemers.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s first line in Qur’anic form: harm settles on those who cause it.
islam.source: Qur’an 35:43 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Very close to the Kural’s first line; does not draw the second line’s practical advice.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made. His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist says the evildoer falls into his own trap and his violence comes down on his own head.
judaism.tie_back: Both declare that the pain one causes lands on oneself.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on harm returning to its author; lacks the explicit advice to abstain in order to be free of suffering.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If on the hand there is no wound, one may carry even poison in it. Poison does not affect one who is free from wounds. For him who does no evil, there is no ill.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the one who does no evil to a hand without cuts: poison cannot harm it.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s second line: the person who does no harm stays free of harm.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close: freedom from ill for those who do no evil.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He does mischief to himself who does mischief to another, and evil planned harms the plotter most.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns his brother Perses that anyone who harms another is really harming himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s central claim in Greek form: pain caused to others falls on the one who causes it.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 265–266 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match of the Kural’s first line. Hesiod is a didactic poet rather than a mythographer, but the work is the chief source of early Greek myth-based ethics.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Does any one do wrong? It is to himself that he does the wrong.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius reminds himself that the wrongdoer is the real victim of his own wrong.
philosophy.tie_back: Both place the harm of wrongdoing on the one who commits it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close to the Kural’s first line; the harm is understood as damage to one’s own character.
